 University navigates class disruptions due to weather, air quality concerns
 By Stephanie Dana Fabia , Ingrid Sampang and Summer Tan Gana 
 Published November 11, 2026 at 8:00 pm 
 Share to: Photo by RJ Hernandez
 19 DAYS of classes in the Ateneo undergraduate schools were suspended or shifted online during the first semester of AY 2026–2027 due to heavy rainfall and unhealthy air quality, prompting faculty to adjust academic schedules and students to navigate challenges to learning continuity.
 At the start of the semester, classes were fully suspended on August 5 , 8 , and 13 due to heavy rainfall brought by the Southwest Monsoon. Meanwhile, 16 class days transitioned to online modalities as inclement weather persisted and air quality levels deteriorated.
 These disruptions have raised concerns among faculty members and students over maintaining learning momentum and meeting the required 45 contact-hours for a standard three-unit course, including at least 30 hours of onsite instruction.
 Institutional adaptation 
 Onsite classes are automatically suspended when the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration raises Typhoon Signal No. 3 or higher, or when government declarations mandate a shift in learning modality, as outlined in a 2025 memorandum.
 While tropical cyclone wind signals govern severe storm protocols for suspension, the severe precipitation resulting in class disruptions this semester was predominantly driven by the Southwest Monsoon.
 As such, the authority to suspend undergraduate classes rests with Vice President for Higher Education (VPHE) Czarina Saloma-Akpedonu, PhD, in the absence of official government declarations.
 Under the University’s revised 2025 guidelines on cancellation and suspension of classes, announcements for whole-day or morning cancellations must be posted no later than 4:30 AM on the day of the intended suspension, while notices for afternoon suspensions must be released by 11:00 AM through official University channels.
 The guidelines also designate online learning as the default response to onsite class suspensions unless otherwise specified, while allowing “flexibility” based on the circumstances of both instructors and students.
 The number of suspended onsite sessions reportedly impacted Tuesday and Friday classes by “5.5 days more” in the term. To recover these lost onsite contact hours, the administration cancelled the pre-scheduled Faculty Day and converted the semestral study days before final assessments into regular class sessions.
 The GUIDON also sought the VPHE’s insights on the University’s measures to address concerns regarding learning continuity. However, due to Saloma-Akpedonu’s unavailability, the publication submitted written questions instead.
 The office has yet to respond despite subsequent follow-ups before publication.
 Sustainability of suspensions 
 To meet the number of at least 30 onsite learning hours for a three-unit course, Biology Department Chair Ronald Allan Cruz, PhD, shared that some faculty members under his department had to adjust their syllabi by combining activities, shifting exercises online, and modifying laboratory schedules.
 He added that adapting to these shifts have been challenging for departments under the School of Science and Engineering (SOSE) due to the necessary onsite nature of laboratory courses.
 Moving forward, Cruz considers the possibility of conducting supplementary student-teacher workshops due to the missed sessions this semester, as well as “reimagining” exercises to include alternative online modalities.
 “We really have to move toward becoming a resilient University. In many ways, we are, but I think the past few cancellations [...] showed us that we still have to figure out a lot of things with regard to how we handle class suspensions,” he said.
 Ateneo Environmental Science Society President Raliza Guanlao also questioned the University’s protocols regarding announcements on class modality shifts, stating that they are “too inconsistent” in terms of scope and timing.
 “It’s a very multi-sectoral issue, [and] it’s very difficult to pinpoint where to solve the problem and who technically is at fault [when announcing suspensions], because there are so many people who are [involved],” Guanlao stated.
 As such, she called for “collaborative efforts” between the national government, the University, and student body to establish clearer protocols for class suspensions.
 Safety and well-being 
 Beyond adjustments in course requirements, Sanggunian SOSE Disaster and Risk Resilience (DRR) Head Timothy Calimlim highlighted that class disruptions have affected students’ ability to understand lessons due to unequal access to conducive learning areas during online class shifts.
 Amid these concerns, Calimlim shared that the Sanggunian conducts constituency checks through Google Forms and text blasts to assess student welfare. Course representatives and concerned Sanggunian officers then assist moderately to heavily affected students.
 However, Guanlao described the existing constituency checks as “inefficient” in addressing students’ learning needs during inclement weather, noting that keeping up with missed lessons and requirements mainly lay on the students’ own efforts.
 To address this gap, she called for a University-wide system to assess students’ capacity to attend online classes during severe weather, before determining alternative learning modalities.
 Meanwhile, Calimlim disclosed that the DRR unit plans to establish a task force within AY 2026–2027 to strengthen student-administration communication on disaster safety and preparedness.
 He further emphasized the need for a “proactive” and “participatory” system that is “fitted towards the context and needs” of the Ateneo community.
